newsitem.title: USA: Gulf widens between Echostar and News Corp..
newsitem.headline: Gulf widens between Echostar and News Corp..

text.p: EchoStar Communications Corp. filed a federal lawsuit against Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. on Friday, further widening the gap between the two potential partners in a multi billion-dollar satellite television venture.
EchoStar said in a brief statement that it asked the U.S. District Court for Colorado for a declaratory judgment confirming News Corp.'s obligation to loan EchoStar $200 million.
"EchoStar is confident that the court will confirm its position," the company said.
In response to the announcement News Corp. issued a terse statement saying it would contest the court action.
"News Corporation believes there is no merit to Echostar's claim and will vigorously contest this matter," it said in a statement released by its New York office.

Asked if the latest legal development would affect the two companies' plans for a direct-TV satellite network, a spokesman for News Corp. said the company, which is based in Australia, had no comment on that matter.
Wall Street, however, was leary of the latest legal wrangle between the two would-be partners.
Shares of EchoStar fell by $2.25 to $13.125 in afternoon trading on the Nasdaq market while News Corp. was up 25 cents at $18.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.

EchoStar, which makes dishes to receive signals from orbiting satellites, and News Corp. announced in February that they were combining to form a direct-TV satellite network that would offer as many as 500 channels of digital television, Internet services and local-broadcast TV signals to markets nationwide.
As part of the deal News Corp., a huge international media conglomerate, was to invest $1 billion in the venture, which still faces regulatory hurdles and stiff competition from several quarters.

But last week the deal between the two companies seemed to have snagged on a dispute over which company's system would be used to allow subscribers to view only those channels they have paid to watch.
EchoStar, which is based in Englewood, Colo., then delayed regulatory filings in regard to the deal, saying News Corp. wanted it to abandon its current system in favour of one owned by News Corp.

Then on May 2 the head of News Corp.'s ASkyB satellite TV service, Preston Padden, who negotiated the deal with EchoStar, suddenly resigned, creating more doubt about the venture among industry analysts.
At that time, Murdoch, who is chairman of News Corp., was quoted in the Wall Street Journal as saying he would go ahead with launching a satellite TV service, with or without EchoStar.
